title: How Is a Hurricane Born? The 2026 Atlantic Season Has Had Just One So Far
fb_caption: The 2026 Atlantic hurricane season officially ends on 30 November. So far it has produced ten named storms but only one hurricane, Isaias. So how is a hurricane born? Three big ingredients: warm ocean water (about 80°F / 26.5°C or more), spin from the Earth's rotation, and calm winds high up so the storm's tower can stand upright. Forecasters say a strong El Niño kept wind shear high this year. A quiet season is no guarantee, though: it only takes one storm. Have you ever been through a hurricane? Tell us below.
engagement_comment: Quick poll: which hurricane ingredient surprised you most? 1 = warm water, 2 = the Earth's spin, 3 = calm winds high up. Reply with a number!

Explainer (general, evergreen; NOAA / NHC / NOAA AOML hurricane FAQ): sea-surface temperature of about 26.5 °C (80 °F) or more; warm moist air rises, water vapour condenses and releases latent heat; Coriolis effect from the Earth's rotation gives the spin (counter-clockwise in the northern hemisphere; almost none at the equator, so tropical cyclones rarely form within about 5° of it); low vertical wind shear is needed; eye = sinking air, eyewall = strongest winds; Atlantic season 1 June - 30 November, peak mid-August to late October. beats.text: The 2026 Atlantic hurricane season officially ends on November 30th. So far it has produced ten named storms, but only one hurricane: Isaias.
So how is a hurricane born, and why so few this year? Here are the three big ingredients.
One: the ocean has to be warm, about 80 degrees Fahrenheit, 26 and a half Celsius, or more. That warm water is the fuel.

Warm, moist air rises off the sea. As it cools, the vapor condenses into cloud, and that releases heat. The heat makes the air rise even faster, pulling in more moist air below. It works like a heat engine.

Two: the storm needs spin. The Earth's rotation bends the incoming winds, so the whole system starts to turn, counterclockwise north of the equator. Right at the equator there's almost no spin, so hurricanes almost never form there.

items: ALMOST NO SPIN AT THE EQUATOR

beats.text: Three: the winds high up have to be calm. If they change sharply with height, called wind shear, they tip the storm's tower over and it falls apart. This year, forecasters say a strong El Niño kept that shear high.

items: FORECASTERS: EL NIÑO KEPT SHEAR HIGH

beats.text: When all three line up, the storm organizes. Air sinks in the middle and clears a calm eye. Around it stands the eyewall, a ring of towering clouds with the strongest winds.

items: AIR SINKS: A CALM, CLEAR EYE

beats.text: That's why the season peaks from August to October, when the ocean is warmest. By late November the water cools, the shear picks up, and the engine shuts down.
Takeaway: a quiet season is no guarantee. It only takes one storm. So if you live near the coast, know your evacuation zone before next June.

items: A QUIET SEASON IS NO GUARANTEE

beats.text: Have you ever been through a hurricane? Tell us in the comments, and send this to someone who lives near the coast. Because this season is ending with just one.
